messages.subject: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.subject_clean: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I have been conducting line transect counts on Red-neck wallabies in=20
Australia. Because this animal inhabits woodland (low detection distance)=
, and=20
in this region exists at a low density I have been forced to conduct coun=
ts via=20
vehicle to get enough of a sample size.=20

While these tracks and roads are not straight, they are fairly well distr=
ibuted=20
across the vegetation and elevation types found within the reserve=20
(random?). In conducting these counts I have divided roads into sections=20=

(usually less than 5 km) often corresponding to fence boundaries. Wallaby=
=20
counts have then been recorded based on perpendicular distance from each=20=

line segment. In analysing the data I have a number of problems.=20

First, wallaby numbers are highly correlated with certain areas, with enc=
ounter=20
rates of 3-4 per line segment in some areas, but repeat 0=92s on other=20=

segments. To improve precision I resample the high encounter line segment=
s=20
multiple times. However, some zero encounter lines have only been surveye=
d=20
once or twice. I see this as a slight deviation from adaptive sampling, w=
here=20
sampling effort is increased in high encounter areas, however repeat samp=
les=20
are not independent (same line). Do I pool all encounters for each line=20=

segment and treat each line separately? Or can I treat all line visits (p=
seudo=20
replication?) as independent, standardise the number of repeat visits (5 =
per=20
line segment) and assume line segments which recorded zero wallabies on t=
he=20
first two visits will encounter zero for the next three (wallabies are ve=
ry=20
predictable in range, and don=92t travel far)? Of course there are some p=
roblems=20
with the last interpretation regarding pseudo replication, but there is n=
o=20
reason to assume wallabies respond passively or negatively to the roads (=
they=20
are old fire tails which are rarely if ever used) rather they have set te=
rritories=20
that some roads intersect.=20

The last problem is in bias in the allocation of sampling based on transe=
cts. Is=20
it possible to analysis in GIS software using buffers (30m around each=20=

segment) to compare the vegetation sampled by tracks/roads to the overall=
=20
division of vegetation communities? If I have over sampled one particular=
=20
vegetation type adjustments could be made. Thoughts on solving this analy=
sis?
Cheers
Brett

--

messages.subject: Re: Comparison line transect and point transect--subject change

messages.body_plain:
Jim:

A good place to get a reminder of how to enter data (whether line or
point transects), is to look at the sample projects that come with
Distance.  The 'Sample Projects' directory is the default directory that
Distance will examine when you ask to open a project.

For your specific question regarding point transects with no detections,
take a look at the project 'Songbird.dst'  When you look at the data
sheet for that project, you will note that point 17 had no detections.
It has a record at the sample layer (called Point transect), but no
associated records in the observation layer.  There needs to be a record
associated with the point, because you exerted sampling effort, even if
you did not record any detections.

Hope that helps.  Let me know if that answers your question.

messages.subject: Re: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.subject_clean: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brett, List,

Some thoughts, others might have more to add...

In order to use conventional distance sampling methods from roads you=20
have to assume that the distribution of roads is independent of the=20
animal's distribution, as only then you can assume that the distribution=20
of distances from the line to all the animals, detected or not, is on=20
average uniform (a requirement for CDS to work). From your description,=20
it seems like this assumption might be reasonable, but note ultimately=20
this is based on faith unless you collect data to prove it! Further, for=20
the obtained density estimate to be valid in a wider area, you have also=20
to assume that the roads cover a representative (i.e. were a random=20
sample) fraction of the wider survey area.

The clustered nature of the data you mention, per se, is not an issue,=20
as that is often the case. It just means your variance estimates will=20
probably be higher than if the clumping was less severe, but that's=20
life... You can visit areas of higher encounter rate more often, in=20
order to increase your sample size for the detection function=20
estimation, but in such case you have to ensure that you: (1) record the=20
effort appropriately and (2) do not have marked differences in detection=20
in high density and low density areas.

Regarding 1, as you suggest, what you should do is to pool all the=20
sightings you have in any given transect of length Lt, repeated k times,=20
and record the line length as being k*Lt. This tells Distance that you=20
have not been sampling k different transects, but the same transect k=20
times, and therefore Distance can calculate the appropriate variances. A=20
couple of notes: a. Be sure not to weight any global density estimates=20
by transect length, as this would lead to problems; b. note your idea of=20
pretending to have detected 0 animals on visits you have not done seems=20
one you really want to avoid!

Regarding 2, this is likely just being over cautious, but you could hit=20
problems if you had say areas of high density, and areas of low density,=20
  and these also had different detection functions. Then, estimates in=20
subsets of the area might be biased, even though the overall density=20
should be unbiased (as long as pooling robustness holds).

You final question, regarding the use of  a GIS correction: if you think=20
that vegetation might have an impact in density estimates (or the=20
detection function), then you might want to consider MCDS - to account=20
for those differences in g(x) - and, if you really want to get=20
complicated, spatial modeling distance sampling, in which you predict=20
density in the area of interest based on a model, as a function of=20
covariates, rather than based on the properties of your design. This=20
might be a better approach than some other ad hoc correction factor you=20
obtain based on buffer areas around the sampled roads.

Cheers,

Tiago

messages.subject: Re: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.subject_clean: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brett, List,

Some thoughts, others might have more to add...

In order to use conventional distance sampling methods from roads you=20
have to assume that the distribution of roads is independent of the=20
animal's distribution, as only then you can assume that the distribution=20
of distances from the line to all the animals, detected or not, is on=20
average uniform (a requirement for CDS to work). From your description,=20
it seems like this assumption might be reasonable, but note ultimately=20
this is based on faith unless you collect data to prove it! Further, for=20
the obtained density estimate to be valid in a wider area, you have also=20
to assume that the roads cover a representative (i.e. were a random=20
sample) fraction of the wider survey area.

The clustered nature of the data you mention, per se, is not an issue,=20
as that is often the case. It just means your variance estimates will=20
probably be higher than if the clumping was less severe, but that's=20
life... You can visit areas of higher encounter rate more often, in=20
order to increase your sample size for the detection function=20
estimation, but in such case you have to ensure that you: (1) record the=20
effort appropriately and (2) do not have marked differences in detection=20
in high density and low density areas.

Regarding 1, as you suggest, what you should do is to pool all the=20
sightings you have in any given transect of length Lt, repeated k times,=20
and record the line length as being k*Lt. This tells Distance that you=20
have not been sampling k different transects, but the same transect k=20
times, and therefore Distance can calculate the appropriate variances. A=20
couple of notes: a. Be sure not to weight any global density estimates=20
by transect length, as this would lead to problems; b. note your idea of=20
pretending to have detected 0 animals on visits you have not done seems=20
one you really want to avoid!

Regarding 2, this is likely just being over cautious, but you could hit=20
problems if you had say areas of high density, and areas of low density,=20
  and these also had different detection functions. Then, estimates in=20
subsets of the area might be biased, even though the overall density=20
should be unbiased (as long as pooling robustness holds).

You final question, regarding the use of  a GIS correction: if you think=20
that vegetation might have an impact in density estimates (or the=20
detection function), then you might want to consider MCDS - to account=20
for those differences in g(x) - and, if you really want to get=20
complicated, spatial modeling distance sampling, in which you predict=20
density in the area of interest based on a model, as a function of=20
covariates, rather than based on the properties of your design. This=20
might be a better approach than some other ad hoc correction factor you=20
obtain based on buffer areas around the sampled roads.

Cheers,

Tiago

messages.subject: Re: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.subject_clean: repeat line transect sampling along tracks
messages.body_plain:
Brett, List,

A word of caution regarding my last e-mail. Even if you assume everything=

else is ok with your survey (i.e. animals do not react to roads, roads ar=
e
random within larger area, usual distance sampling assumptions hold, etc)=
,
you might have a problem because you are allocating more effort to high
density areas than to low density areas.

My reply was assuming that these corresponded to 2 different strata (say
"high density" and "low density"). If that was the case, then you could d=
o
as I suggested, you would get a density estimate valid in each stratum
(pooling the detection function, so it assumes the same detection functio=
n
for unbiased within-strata estimates), and you could get a combined densi=
ty
estimate as a weighted (by stratum area) average of the strata estimates.=

The key being you would have the same level of effort across areas within=

strata.

However, if you have only a single area, then you will have trouble to
estimate density, as you have oversampled high density areas, and hence
could potentially severely overestimate density in the area. Possible
alternatives then would involve:

A. post-stratification of areas according to effort, so that effort is th=
e
same within strata.
B. if you have at least 2 visits to all transects, you could use only the=

first two visits data for the encounter rate (hence constant effort) and
then all the visits for the detection function estimation. This would
require  multiple runs of Distance and manually combining the results.

Cheers

Tiago

messages.subject: Introductory distance sampling workshop, California,
messages.subject_clean: Introductory distance sampling workshop, California,
messages.body_plain:
Staff from the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental
Modelling, Univ. of St. Andrews will deliver this workshop hosted by the
Scripps Institute of Oceanography (SIO) this coming summer (12-15 July).
The workshop instructors will be Drs. David Borchers, Len Thomas, and
Tiago Marques. Over 3.5 days, we will focus on distance sampling
methods, as described in the standard reference book Introduction to
Distance Sampling (book will be provided). The workshop will be a blend
of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the
program Distance.

Registration and payment deadline is 1 June; so to hold a place, please
register soon for the remaining places at website
(http://www.cetus.ucsd.edu/Distance.html). This site also contains
information on accommodation (campus housing at UCSD as well as other
negotiated rates) along with information on the location and other details.

Those interested in the application of passive acoustics in abundance
estimation may also attend a SIO symposium the following day
(http://www.cetus.ucsd.edu/Density.html).

--

messages.subject_clean: Introductory distance sampling workshop, California,
messages.body_plain:
Staff from the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental
Modelling, Univ. of St. Andrews will deliver this workshop hosted by the
Scripps Institute of Oceanography (SIO) this coming summer (12-15 July).
The workshop instructors will be Drs. David Borchers, Len Thomas, and
Tiago Marques. Over 3.5 days, we will focus on distance sampling
methods, as described in the standard reference book Introduction to
Distance Sampling (book will be provided). The workshop will be a blend
of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the
program Distance.

Registration and payment deadline is 1 June; so to hold a place, please
register soon for the remaining places at website
(http://www.cetus.ucsd.edu/Distance.html). This site also contains
information on accommodation (campus housing at UCSD as well as other
negotiated rates) along with information on the location and other details.

Those interested in the application of passive acoustics in abundance
estimation may also attend a SIO symposium the following day
(http://www.cetus.ucsd.edu/Density.html).

messages.subject: Ph.D. Assistantship: EFFECTS OF IMPERFECT DETECTABILITY ON
messages.subject_clean: Ph.D. Assistantship: EFFECTS OF IMPERFECT DETECTABILITY ON
messages.body_plain:
EFFECTS OF IMPERFECT DETECTABILITY ON INFERENCES FROM AVIAN MONITORING

Ph.D. ASSISTANTSHIP in WILDLIFE ECOLOGY AND MANAGEMENT or CONSERVATION
BIOLOGY
Minnesota Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit
University of Minnesota, St. Paul, Minnesota

PROJECT DESCRIPTION: The value of bird monitoring has come under
increasing scrutiny recently due to concerns about imperfect
detectability.  In particular, because the probability of detecting a bird
in the area surveyed often is less than one, counts are indices of
abundance, rather than actual estimates of abundance.  Although a variety
of methods that attempt to adjust counts for imperfect detectability have
been advanced, questions arise about the applicability of the methods in
extensive multispecies surveys.  A critical question is the extent to
which estimates of population change are affected by imperfect
detectability and whether or not suggested adjustment methods offer
improved results worthy of the additional effort.  The objective of the
proposed study is to evaluate the influence of imperfect detectability on
inferences about population changes.

The student is expected to simulate a wide variety of conditions involving
detectability (both availability and perceptibility) and determine how
inferences about trends would be affected.  Detectability will be varied
in realistic ways, as indicated by field observations and controlled
studies.  Simulated results will be adjusted for detectability in
accordance with suggested procedures (various distance sampling,
multiple-observer, and time-to-detection methods).  As necessary, field
studies will be conducted to determine how detectability is affected by
abundance and variety of birds and other features.

REQUISITES: M.S. or M.A. in a scientific or mathematical field.
(Alternatively, a B.A. or B.S. along with strong evidence that the student
could successfully complete a Ph.D. program.) Quantitative and
computational skills; an interest in avian biology and conservation;
ability to work with diverse project cooperators; ability to help design
and conduct simulation studies and field research; and meet or exceed
program entry requirements in Natural Resources Science and Management
(Wildlife Ecology and Management track) or Conservation Biology at the
University of Minnesota.

DESIRED EXPERIENCE: Previous field work with or surveys of birds,
demonstrated quantitative and data analysis skills, and previous
peer-reviewed publications.

DURATION: As soon as suitable candidate is found, continuing for three
years.

STIPEND: About $18,800 per year, plus health insurance and tuition waiver

CONTACT:

Fisheries, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology

1980 Folwell Avenue
St. Paul, MN  55108

messages.subject: Surveys which combine both point and line transects
messages.subject_clean: Surveys which combine both point and line transects
messages.body_plain:
I am currently working on a dataset of opportunistic distance sightings from
a marine mammal monitoring program. My aim is to create a Generalized
Additive Model which will allow me to predict density and distribution of
cetaceans within my study area. Because the vessel both travels through the
study area and spends time monitoring vessel activity around killer whales
there are times when the vessel is traveling at different speeds. I can
determine when the vessel was monitoring and when they were transiting. As
such, I wondered if it made sense to analyze the sightings collected when
monitoring (travelling at less than 5 knots) as point transects in Distance
and when the vessel is transiting to analyze them as line transects. The
difficulty with this is that I am not sure how this will affect how I build
the model as I will have different detection functions depending on what the
vessel is doing?

I was also wondering if one way to tackle this issue would be to use vessel
speed as a covariate in the MCDS function of Distance - or if that is at all
appropriate.

Any thoughts on this would be much appreciated.

Thank You
Nicole

--
Nicole Koshure
Master's Candidate
Fisheries Research Group
School of Resource and Environmental Management
Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, BC
nm...@sfu.ca

--
